subject: Accounting
title: Sarbanes-Oxley Changed Everything
description: A fast breakdown of Sarbanes-Oxley Changed Everything for builders.

hook.text: After Enron and WorldCom, Congress passed the toughest corporate accountability law in history.

buildup.text: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 required CEO certification, internal controls, and auditor oversight.

discovery.text: It created the PCAOB—a new body to inspect and regulate audit firms for the first time.

twist.text: Compliance costs billions annually. Some companies went private or listed overseas to avoid it.

climax.text: Love it or hate it, SOX restored enough confidence for markets to recover and grow.

punchline.text: Scandal wrote the rules. Markets needed them.

quiz.question: What did the Sarbanes-Oxley Act create?
options: The PCAOB to oversee audit firms

details.summary: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 was enacted in response to Enron, WorldCom, and other scandals, creating the most significant overhaul of US securities regulation since the 1930s. This topic covers SOX's key provisions and its lasting impact on corporate accountability.
details.whyItMatters: SOX transformed corporate governance in America. CEOs now personally certify financial statements, internal controls are mandatory, and an independent board oversees all auditors of public companies.
takeaways: CEOs and CFOs must personally certify the accuracy of financial statements under penalty of prison
Section 404 requires companies to document, test, and report on internal controls over financial reporting
The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board was created to regulate the audit profession

faq.question: What is the Sarbanes-Oxley Act?
faq.answer: Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) is a 2002 US law that imposed strict governance requirements on public companies following the Enron and WorldCom scandals. Key provisions include CEO/CFO certification of financials, mandatory internal control testing, and creation of the PCAOB.

faq.question: What is Section 404 of Sarbanes-Oxley?
faq.answer: Section 404 requires management to assess and report on the effectiveness of internal controls over financial reporting, and requires the external auditor to attest to that assessment. It is the most costly and controversial provision, but also the most impactful for fraud prevention.
